claim: Three CheY-like response regulators (CC1364, CC2249, and CC3100) were isolated from C. crescentus cell extracts using c-di-GMP specific Capture Compound mass-spectrometry (CCMS).
source: Using c-di-GMP specific Capture Compound (cdG-CC) in combination with mass-spectrometry (CCMS) (Nesper et al., 2012; Laventie et al., 2015) we isolated three CheY-like response regulators, CC1364, CC2249 and CC3100, from C. crescentus cell extracts (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data from CCMS experiments presented in Table 1, and references established methods from prior publications.

claim: The three isolated CheY-like proteins group together with two additional CheY-like proteins (CC0440, CC3155) in a branch of the CheY/CheB related chemotaxis cluster based on phylogenetic analysis.
source: A phylogenetic analysis of all C. crescentus receiver domains revealed that these proteins group together with two additional CheY-like proteins (CC0440, CC3155) in a branch of the CheY/CheB related chemotaxis cluster (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The CheY-like protein subcluster is distinguished by short C-terminal extensions containing a conserved arginine-rich region (ARR) and a C-terminal region (CTR) of variable length and sequence identity.
source: This subcluster was classified before based on short C-terminal extensions, which distinguish them from canonical CheY proteins (Galperin, 2004). This extension can be subdivided into a conserved arginine-rich region (ARR) and a C-terminal region (CTR) of variable length and sequence identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by prior classification work (citation to Galperin, 2004) and alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Members of the CheY-like protein family specifically bind c-di-GMP and this second messenger controls their activity.
source: Below we present evidence that members of this family specifically bind c-di-GMP and that this second messenger controls their activity. We thus renamed these proteins CheY-like c-di-GMP effectors CleA (CC0440), CleB (CC1364), CleC (CC2249), CleD (CC3100) and CleE (CC3155).
evidence: The claim is stated explicitly and is supported by experimental evidence presented later in the manuscript.

claim: CleD binds c-di-GMP with high affinity in the nanomolar range as determined by UV cross-linking experiments.
source: UV cross-linking experiments with purified Strep-tagged CleD and radiolabeled c-di-GMP revealed high affinity binding in the nanomolar range (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by UV cross-linking experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: CleD binds c-di-GMP with a Kd of 86 nM as determined by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).
source: High affinity binding was confirmed by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments revealing a Kd of 86 nM (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: CleD binds c-di-GMP specifically, as unlabeled c-di-GMP but not related nucleotides effectively compete with labeled probe for binding.
source: CleD binds c-di-GMP specifically as unlabeled c-di-GMP but not related nucleotides were able to effectively compete with the labeled probe for binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition binding experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Two molecules of c-di-GMP bind to one CleD protomer as indicated by NMR spectroscopy showing four imino proton H1 resonances.
source: When recording the difference spectrum of CleD with and without c-di-GMP, the four imino proton H1 resonances were found far downfield shifted (between 14ppm and 10.5ppm), indicating that two molecules of c-di-GMP are bound to one CleD protomer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CleD protein is a monomer in both its apo- and ligand-bound forms as determined by multi-angle light scattering (MALS) experiments.
source: Finally, multi-angle light scattering (MALS) experiments indicated that the CleD protein is a monomer both in its apo- and ligand-bound forms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by MALS experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: CleD is a member of a novel family of CheY-like proteins that bind c-di-GMP with high affinity and specificity.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrated that CleD is a member of a novel family of CheY-like proteins that bind c-di-GMP with high affinity and specificity.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results (UV cross-linking, ITC, NMR, MALS) presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Kd of full-length CleD for 2'fluoro-AHC-c-di-GMP (flr-cdG) is 1.2 μM as determined by microscale thermophoresis (MST).
source: The Kd values of full-length CleD and a variant lacking part of the CTR were determined as 1.2 μM and 1.3 μM, respectively (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The dissociation constant of CleD Rec-ARR variant for flr-cdG is 5-fold higher (6.2 µM) compared to full-length protein.
source: The dissociation constant of the Rec-ARR variant was 5-fold higher (6.2 µM), while the dissociation constant of the Rec domain alone was increased by 40-fold (41.7 µM) as compared to the full-length protein (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The dissociation constant of CleD Rec domain alone for flr-cdG is 40-fold higher (41.7 µM) compared to full-length protein.
source: The dissociation constant of the Rec-ARR variant was 5-fold higher (6.2 µM), while the dissociation constant of the Rec domain alone was increased by 40-fold (41.7 µM) as compared to the full-length protein (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The ARR of CleD is sufficient for c-di-GMP binding when fused to E. coli CheY, with a Kd of 14.8 µM for flr-cdG.
source: While purified E. coli CheY protein failed to bind flr-cdG, the chimeric EcCheY-ARR protein bound flr-cdG with a Kd of 14.8 µM (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: E. coli CheY fused to CleD ARR binds c-di-GMP with a Kd of 150 nM and 2:1 binding stoichiometry as determined by ITC.
source: ITC experiments with EcCheY-ARR revealed a Kd of 150 nM for c-di-GMP and a 2:1 binding stoichiometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: All ARR peptides of Cle proteins (CleB, CleC, CleD, CleE) bind flr-cdG when fused to His-SUMO.
source: As shown in Figure 3c we found that all ARRs but not SUMO itself were able to bind flr-cdG. The only exception was CleA, the isolated ARR of which failed to bind flr-cdG, but showed binding when purified together with its CTR.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: CleA ARR alone fails to bind flr-cdG, but shows binding when purified together with its CTR.
source: The only exception was CleA, the isolated ARR of which failed to bind flr-cdG, but showed binding when purified together with its CTR.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The short C-terminal ARR extensions of Cle proteins are high-affinity binding modules for c-di-GMP that retain their binding properties when grafted onto a heterologous carrier protein.
source: Thus, these experiments disclosed the short C-terminal ARR extensions of Cle proteins as high-affinity binding modules for c-di-GMP that retain their binding properties when grafted onto a heterologous carrier protein.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing ARR peptides can bind c-di-GMP when fused to SUMO or E. coli CheY.

claim: Homologous ARR sequences were found in a total of 302 bacterial proteins using iterative search approaches with Jackhmmer and PSI-Blast.
source: Using the ARR sequence of CleD as query, we found homologous sequences in a total of 302 bacterial proteins including 294 from alphaproteobacteria, three from Cyanobacteria species and five from unclassified bacteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: 91% of proteins with ARR sequences are CheY homologs with a single Rec domain and a C-terminal ARR.
source: Most of these proteins (91%) are CheY homologs with a single Rec domain and a C-terminal ARR.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatics analysis of proteins identified through sequence searches.

claim: The ARR sequences contain a conserved motif [Y/F]XGP[D/E][R/K]R arranged in tandem as a core feature.
source: This revealed a conserved motif [Y/F]XGP[D/E][R/K]R arranged in tandem as core feature of the ARR sequences flanked by a highly conserved Arg at the N- and an Asp at the C-terminus (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The R156A mutant of CleD ARR shows strongly reduced binding to flr-cdG with a Kd of 471 μM when fused to E. coli CheY.
source: Indeed, the R156A mutant peptide showed strongly reduced binding to flr-cdG in MST experiments either when fused to CheY from E. coli (Kd471 μM) (Figure 3b) or when fused to SUMO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Binding to the R156A mutant of CleD ARR was completely abolished, while binding to the R169A mutant was reduced about 5-fold.
source: Binding to the R156A mutant was completely abolished, while binding to the R169A mutant was reduced about 5-fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by MST and ITC experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: Mutating R113 to Ala in CleD resulted in a 3-fold increase of the Kd (221 nM) compared to wild-type CleD (86 nM).
source: Mutating the corresponding residue R113 of CleD to Ala resulted in a 3-fold increase of the Kd (221 nM) as compared to wild-type CleD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The Rec domain may contribute to c-di-GMP binding in vivo.
source: Thus, the Rec domain may contribute to c-di-GMP binding in vivo (see below).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation that R113 mutation affects binding affinity.

claim: The conserved Arg residues of the ARR peptide define a core motif for c-di-GMP binding in the Cle protein family.
source: Together, these data define a core motif for c-di-GMP binding in the Arg-rich peptide of the Cle protein family.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on mutagenesis and binding studies showing the importance of conserved Arg residues.

claim: CleA-mGFPmut3 was found at one cell pole in about 30% of cells while 60% of cells showed diffuse cytoplasmic localization.
source: CleA was found at one cell pole in about 30% of the cells while 60% of the cells showed diffuse cytoplasmic localization (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: CleA-mGFPmut3 foci were observed primarily at the pole opposite the stalk of late PD cells and in SW cells.
source: CleA-mGFPmut3 foci were observed primarily at the pole opposite the stalk of late PD cells and in SW cells, arguing that CleA dynamically positions to the C. crescentus flagellated pole immediately before and after cell division.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by fluorescence microscopy observations and includes an inference about dynamic positioning.

claim: CleD-eGFP was localized to the flagellated pole in roughly 30% of PD and swarmer cells.
source: Similarly, CleD-eGFP was localized to the flagellated pole in roughly 30% of PD and swarmer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: An intact c-di-GMP binding site in the ARR peptide is required for the localization of CleA and CleD to the flagellated cell pole.
source: This indicated that an intact c-di-GMP binding site in the ARR peptide is required for the localization of CleA and CleD to the flagellated cell pole.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the observation that mutants lacking central Arg residues of the ARR peptide failed to localize to the pole.

claim: The fliM_ID57WA mutant maintains overall motility and swimming speed but cells fail to reverse their swimming direction.
source: When the highly conserved Ile/Asp motif at position 57/58 of FliM was replaced with a bulky Trp and an uncharged Ala residue, respectively, overall motility and swimming speed was maintained but cells failed to reverse their swimming direction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: CleA and CleD failed to localize in the fliM_ID57WA mutant.
source: Importantly, CleA and CleD also failed to localize in the fliM_ID57WA mutant (Figure 4b; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Bacterial two-hybrid assays showed strong interaction of CleA with the N-terminal peptide of FliM (amino acid 2 to 65) but not with the FliMID57WA mutant peptide.
source: Moreover, bacterial two-hybrid assays (Karimova et al., 1998) showed strong interaction of CleA with the N-terminal peptide of FliM (amino acid 2 to 65) but not with the FliMID57WA mutant peptide (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by bacterial two-hybrid experimental data shown in Figure 4c and references the method.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments showed co-purification of CleD-Flag with FliM.
source: Although bacterial two-hybrid experiments failed to show interaction between CleD and FliM, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiments showed co-purification of CleD-Flag with FliM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NMR experiments confirmed CleD binding to synthetic FliM peptides corresponding to residues 47 to 62 of FliM in the presence of c-di-GMP.
source: Likewise, NMR experiments confirmed CleD binding to synthetic FliM peptides corresponding to residues 47 to 62 of FliM. A 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of 15N-CleD was recorded alone and in the presence of c-di-GMP and the FliM wild-type peptide in two-fold excess. The latter resulted in shift changes of CleD of approximately 10 resonances (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Neither the addition of the FliMID57WA mutant peptide with c-di-GMP nor the FliM wild-type peptide without c-di-GMP gave an observable chemical shift in NMR experiments with CleD.
source: In contrast, neither the addition of the FliMID57WA mutant peptide with c-di-GMP nor the FliM wild-type peptide without c-di-GMP gave an observable chemical shift.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by NMR spectroscopy data described in the text.

claim: CleA and CleD bind to the FliM switch protein in a way that is similar or identical to CheY docking to the flagellar motor.
source: Thus, CleA and CleD bind to the FliM switch protein in a way that is similar or identical to CheY docking to the flagellar motor.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental evidence showing interaction with the conserved CheY binding motif on FliM.

claim: The interaction of CleA and CleD with FliM is regulated by c-di-GMP binding.
source: Based on this and on the data shown above, we conclude that this interaction is regulated by c-di-GMP binding to CleA and CleD.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined evidence that c-di-GMP binding is required for polar localization and that localization depends on FliM interaction.

claim: Strains with single cle deletions showed increased spreading on semisolid agar plates.
source: Strains with single cle deletions showed increased spreading on semisolid agar plates (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Spreading increased almost four-fold in a mutant lacking all five Cle proteins on semisolid agar plates.
source: Strikingly, spreading increased almost four-fold in a mutant lacking all five Cle proteins (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A mutant lacking CheYII showed very poor spreading on semisolid agar plates.
source: Indeed, a mutant lacking CheYII, the prototypical C. crescentus CheY encoded in the che1 cluster (Ely et al., 1986) (Figure 1b) showed very poor spreading on semisolid agar plates (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5a and references prior work.

claim: The ΔcheR mutant showed strongly reduced reversal rates.
source: In accordance with their role in chemotaxis (Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012) the ΔcheR mutant showed strongly reduced reversal rates (Briegel et al., 2011), while the ΔcheB mutant had increased reversal rates (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 5b and references prior work.

claim: The ΔcheB mutant had increased reversal rates.
source: In accordance with their role in chemotaxis (Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012) the ΔcheR mutant showed strongly reduced reversal rates (Briegel et al., 2011), while the ΔcheB mutant had increased reversal rates (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The ΔcleA mutant and a strain lacking all five Cle proteins (ΔcleA-E) showed strongly increased reversal frequencies and reduced swimming speeds.
source: The ΔcleA mutant and a strain lacking all five Cle proteins (ΔcleA-E) showed strongly increased reversal frequencies and reduced swimming speeds (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Tethered cells of the cleA deletion strain had strongly increased reversal rates as compared to the cleA+ control strain.
source: Likewise, tethered cells of the cleA deletion strain had strongly increased reversal rates as compared to the cleA+ control strain (Video 1,  Video 2).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by tethered cell analysis data shown in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Strains lacking CleD or lacking all Cle proteins except CleA showed normal reversal frequencies.
source: In contrast, strains lacking CleD or lacking all Cle proteins except CleA showed normal reversal frequencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: CleA promotes smooth swimming by antagonizing the major C. crescentus CheY, CheYII.
source: CleA promotes smooth swimming by antagonizing the major C. crescentus CheY, CheYII. Analysis of reversal frequencies and mean speed of the strains indicated was as in (b). It should be noted that the reversal frequency profiles of strains ΔcheYII, DcheYIIΔcleA and ΔcheYIIΔcheYI overlay.
evidence: The claim is supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 5c and epistasis analysis.

claim: A mutant lacking CheYII showed significantly reduced reversal rates.
source: Consistent with a major role in chemotaxis, a mutant lacking CheYII was unable to spread on semisolid agar plates (Skerker et al., 2005) (Figure 5a) and showed significantly reduced reversal rates (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 5c and references prior work.

claim: A cheYI mutant exhibited a hyper-reversal phenotype, akin to the cleA mutant, but with no significant drop in swimming speed.
source: In contrast, a cheYI mutant exhibited a hyper-reversal phenotype, akin to the cleA mutant, but with no significant drop in swimming speed (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Double mutants lacking CheYII and either CheYI or CleA performed poorly on motility plates and showed reduced reversal rates, similar to the cheYII mutant.
source: Importantly, double mutants lacking CheYII and either CheYI or CleA, performed poorly on motility plates (Figure 5a) and showed reduced reversal rates, similar to the cheYII mutant (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by motility assay and swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figures 5a, 5c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: CheYII is the major CheY protein involved in C. crescentus chemotaxis.
source: From these data, we concluded that CheYII is the major CheY protein involved in C. crescentus chemotaxis and that CleA, together with CheYI, modulates motor reversals, possibly by competing with CheYII for the same motor binding sites.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on epistasis analysis and swimming behavior data.

claim: CleA, together with CheYI, modulates motor reversals, possibly by competing with CheYII for the same motor binding sites.
source: From these data, we concluded that CheYII is the major CheY protein involved in C. crescentus chemotaxis and that CleA, together with CheYI, modulates motor reversals, possibly by competing with CheYII for the same motor binding sites.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on epistasis analysis and swimming behavior data, with a speculative mechanism.

claim: A mutant lacking all Cle proteins (ΔcleA-E) showed severely impaired attachment in microfluidic-based assays under flow.
source: A mutant lacking all Cle proteins (ΔcleA-E) showed severely impaired attachment. When cleC, cleD or cleE were expressed in trans surface colonization of the ΔcleA-E strain was restored (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by microfluidic attachment assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: When cleC, cleD or cleE were expressed in trans, surface colonization of the ΔcleA-E strain was restored.
source: When cleC, cleD or cleE were expressed in trans surface colonization of the ΔcleA-E strain was restored (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by microfluidic attachment assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Restoring surface attachment under flow conditions required a motor with intact FliM docking sites for Cle proteins.
source: Importantly, restoring surface attachment under these conditions required a motor with intact FliM docking sites for Cle proteins (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by microfluidic attachment assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Wild-type cells generally deployed a visible holdfast within 1–2 min after separating from their mothers in quasi-2D micro-chambers.
source: Hence, wild-type cells generally deployed a visible holdfast within 1–2 min after separating from their mothers, while cells lacking a functional motor (motBD33N) (Zhou et al., 1998; Kojima and Blair, 2001) showed a significant delay in holdfast formation (Figure 6d) (Hug et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by microfluidic holdfast timing assay data shown in Figure 6d and references prior work.

claim: Cells lacking a functional motor (motBD33N) showed a significant delay in holdfast formation in quasi-2D micro-chambers.
source: Hence, wild-type cells generally deployed a visible holdfast within 1–2 min after separating from their mothers, while cells lacking a functional motor (motBD33N) (Zhou et al., 1998; Kojima and Blair, 2001) showed a significant delay in holdfast formation (Figure 6d) (Hug et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by microfluidic holdfast timing assay data shown in Figure 6d and references prior work.

claim: Mutants devoid of the Cle proteins (ΔcleA-E) or cells lacking a functional Cle docking site on FliM (fliMID57WA) showed delayed holdfast formation in quasi-2D micro-chambers.
source: Mutants devoid of the Cle proteins (ΔcleA-E) or cells lacking a functional Cle docking site on FliM (fliMID57WA) showed delayed holdfast formation.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by microfluidic holdfast timing assay data described in the text and shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Epistasis analysis revealed that the motor is dominant over cle deletions, arguing that Cle proteins are not essential for mechanosensation per se, but rather improve the efficiency of the surface response.
source: Importantly, epistasis analysis revealed that the motor is dominant over cle deletions, arguing that Cle proteins are not essential for mechanosensation per se, but rather improve the efficiency of the surface response (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on epistasis analysis of holdfast formation timing data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: A subset of the Cle proteins interacts with the flagellar motor to promote rapid surface attachment of C. crescentus swarmer cells.
source: Together, these data suggested that a subset of the Cle proteins interacts with the flagellar motor to promote rapid surface attachment of C. crescentus swarmer cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined microfluidic attachment and holdfast formation data.

claim: Expression of wild-type cleA and the cleA_D67A allele restored running speed and low reversal frequencies of a ΔcleA mutant under free-swimming conditions.
source: Expression of wild-type cleA and the cleA_D67A allele restored running speed and low reversal frequencies of a ΔcleA mutant under free-swimming condition in a homogeneous environment (Figure 7b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The cleA_RR153AA allele was non-functional, indicating that c-di-GMP binding is important for CleA function.
source: In contrast, the cleA_RR153AA allele was non-functional indicating that c-di-GMP binding is important for CleA function.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by swimming behavior analysis data and includes an inference about the importance of c-di-GMP binding.

claim: R111 seems to contribute partially to CleA function.
source: Likewise, R111 seems to contribute partially to CleA function (Figure 7c, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by swimming behavior analysis data shown in Figure 7c and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Expression of the cleD_E70A allele reduced motility, demonstrating that this CleD variant is fully functional.
source: Likewise, expression of the cleD_E70A allele reduced motility, demonstrating that this CleD variant is fully functional.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by motility assay data described in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: An intact ARR and the highly conserved Arg in helix α4 were strictly required for CleD function.
source: In contrast, an intact ARR and the highly conserved Arg in helix α4 were strictly required for CleD function (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CleA and CleD are activated by c-di-GMP binding, while conserved residues of the phosphorylation-mediated receiver domain switch are dispensable for Cle activation.
source: In summary, these results demonstrated that CleA and CleD are activated by c-di-GMP binding, while conserved residues of the phosphorylation-mediated receiver domain switch (Volkman et al., 2001) are dispensable for Cle activation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on functional analysis of various CleA and CleD mutants and references prior work on receiver domain switches.

claim: Cle proteins have lost their association with CheA-mediated phosphorylation and instead have adopted c-di-GMP-mediated control by the acquisition of the C-terminal ARR peptide.
source: We speculate that Cle proteins have lost their association with CheA-mediated phosphorylation and instead have adopted c-di-GMP-mediated control by the acquisition of the C-terminal ARR peptide.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation based on the functional data showing c-di-GMP dependence and phosphorylation independence.

claim: All five Cle proteins interact with the polar flagellar motor, possibly in a cooperative or competitive manner with conventional CheY proteins.
source: Given the strong conservation and clustering of these proteins with other C. crescentus CheY proteins, we propose that all five Cle proteins interact with the polar flagellar motor, possibly in a cooperative or competitive manner with conventional CheY proteins (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on sequence conservation and clustering analysis, with a speculative mechanism.

claim: The tandem arrangement of the Arg-containing motifs together with the binding affinity and stoichiometry determined for CleD suggested that all Cle proteins bind a dimer of c-di-GMP.
source: The tandem arrangement of the Arg-containing motifs together with the binding affinity and stoichiometry determined for CleD suggested that all Cle proteins bind a dimer of c-di-GMP and that conserved Arg residues play a central role in this process.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the structural motif analysis and binding stoichiometry data.

claim: Conserved Arg residues play a central role in c-di-GMP binding by Cle proteins.
source: The tandem arrangement of the Arg-containing motifs together with the binding affinity and stoichiometry determined for CleD suggested that all Cle proteins bind a dimer of c-di-GMP and that conserved Arg residues play a central role in this process.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on mutagenesis data showing the importance of Arg residues for binding.

claim: It is plausible that the rearrangement of the ARR peptide via a specific c-di-GMP docking site in helix α4 remodels the α4-β5-α5 surface of Cle proteins to promote its interaction with the motor switch.
source: In analogy, it is plausible that the rearrangement of the ARR peptide via a specific c-di-GMP docking site in helix α4 remodels the α4-β5-α5 surface of Cle proteins to promote its interaction with the motor switch.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a plausible mechanism based on analogy to CheY activation.

claim: Such a mechanism would abrogate the need for phosphorylation-mediated structural changes, explaining why Cle proteins no longer depend on conserved residues of the phospho-switch.
source: Such a mechanism would abrogate the need for phosphorylation-mediated structural changes, explaining why Cle proteins no longer depend on conserved residues of the phospho-switch (Gao and Stock, 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the observed phosphorylation independence, referencing prior work on phospho-switches.

claim: Individual Cle proteins have distinct functions in motility and surface adaptation, suggesting that they represent discrete signaling pathways affecting motor activity.
source: Phenotypic analysis revealed that individual Cle proteins have distinct functions in motility and surface adaptation, suggesting that they represent discrete signaling pathways affecting motor activity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the differential phenotypes observed for different cle mutants.

claim: Individual Cle proteins may differ in their interaction with the motor or with conventional CheYs.
source: Individual Cle proteins may differ in their interaction with the motor or with conventional CheYs.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation to explain functional differences.

claim: The specific functions of Cle proteins may involve their distinct C-terminal extensions, which could help sequester partner proteins with specific functionality to the motor.
source: The specific functions of Cle proteins may involve their distinct C-terminal extensions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), which could help sequester partner proteins with specific functionality to the motor.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation based on sequence variation in C-terminal extensions.

claim: All five cle genes are expressed in PD cells, coincident with the transcription of flagellar and chemotaxis genes.
source: All five cle genes are expressed in PD cells, coincident with the transcription of flagellar and chemotaxis genes (Schrader et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data from cited references.

claim: The concentration of c-di-GMP fluctuates during the cell cycle with c-di-GMP being low in SW cells and reaching peak levels during the SW-to-ST cell transition.
source: The concentration of c-di-GMP fluctuates during the cell cycle with c-di-GMP being low in SW cells and reaching peak levels during the SW-to-ST cell transition (Abel et al., 2013; Christen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by prior work on c-di-GMP dynamics cited in the references.

claim: Recent evidence suggested that c-di-GMP is not evenly distributed in dividing cells with a spatial trough being established at the pole where the flagellum is assembled.
source: Recent evidence suggested that c-di-GMP is not evenly distributed in dividing cells with a spatial trough being established at the pole where the flagellum is assembled (Lori et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by prior work on c-di-GMP spatial distribution cited in the reference.
